Tacit: Chapter ten. Tacit collusion and the law.

The cartel of chapter eight held its price high without anyone agreeing to anything. Each firm simply expected the others to punish a cut. Economists call this tacit collusion. The law forbids something narrower. America's Sherman Act of 1890 and the European Union's Article one hundred and one forbid agreements, and practices concerted between firms, that restrain competition. Parallel prices alone are not enough, because rivals facing the same costs move together anyway. In Bell Atlantic against Twombly, in 2007, the American Supreme Court held that a complaint must allege facts suggesting an agreement, not just parallel behaviour. And in the Wood Pulp case of 1993, the European Court of Justice held that parallel pricing proves concertation only if nothing else can explain it. So the law reaches what firms say to each other, but not what they merely expect of each other.

Some business practices make tacit collusion easier without a word being said. Take a promise to match any lower price. It sounds like a gift to customers, but it is also a message to rivals. Suppose both yards post the monopoly's fifty-five dollars, each promising to match any lower price. Each earns a thousand and twelve dollars fifty. If Crusoe cuts to fifty-four, Dara matches at once, the yards split the island at the lower price, and Crusoe earns a little less. Undercutting no longer wins a single customer, so Bertrand's war never starts. Announcing price rises in advance, and sharing databases of each other's prices, can work the same way.

Where does signalling end and agreement begin? In December 1992 the Justice Department sued eight airlines and the Airline Tariff Publishing Company, the fare database they owned. It alleged that the airlines used the database's first and last ticket dates and its fare footnotes to negotiate the end of each other's discounts: posting fares that would start only weeks later, and withdrawing or matching them before anyone could buy one. It was a conversation held in fares, with offers, replies and agreements. The cases were settled by consent decrees in 1993 and 1994, which forbade fare codes that carry any other message. What happens when the conversation is between pricing algorithms is chapter sixteen's question.

One suspected sign of tacit coordination is found at the petrol pump. Drivers say that prices rise like rockets and fall like feathers. In 1997 Severin Borenstein, Colin Cameron and Richard Gilbert found that American retail prices did respond faster to rises in crude oil than to falls, and suggested inventory lags and the market power of some sellers as reasons. Agora tried the same question on the Data Room's monthly prices since 1986, measuring the pump price's response to each dollar of crude per gallon. In the first month, the pump moves 77 cents after a rise, and 75 cents after a fall: a difference of about 1 cent, with a standard error of 11. Monthly averages blur what happens within a few weeks, so this data cannot settle the question either way, which is a lesson about data as much as about petrol.
